final_note: You worked through Forces and motion: Forces and braking — 20 specification statements.

concepts.def: The total distance a vehicle travels from the moment the driver sees a hazard to the moment the vehicle comes to rest. It is the sum of the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time (thinking distance) and the distance travelled under the braking force (braking distance): stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.

The distance the vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes are applied. The vehicle is still moving at its original speed throughout, so thinking distance = speed x reaction time. It is therefore directly proportional to speed: double the speed and the thinking distance doubles.

The distance the vehicle travels under the braking force, measured from the moment the brakes are applied to the moment the vehicle stops. It depends on the speed, the braking force, the road and weather conditions and the condition of the vehicle's brakes and tyres.

concepts.term: Effect of speed on stopping distance
concepts.def: For a given braking force the greater the speed of the vehicle, the greater the stopping distance. Both parts grow: the thinking distance grows in proportion to speed, and the braking distance grows more steeply still, because the work the brakes must do equals the kinetic energy of the vehicle, and kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed.

Reaction times vary from person to person. Typical values range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s. That spread matters on the road: at 13 m/s (about 30 mph) a reaction time of 0.2 s gives a thinking distance of about 2.6 m, while 0.9 s gives about 12 m from the same speed.

concepts.term: Factors affecting a driver's reaction time
concepts.def: A driver's reaction time can be affected by tiredness, drugs and alcohol. Each of these lengthens the reaction time, so at any given speed they lengthen the thinking distance and therefore the stopping distance. They do not change the braking distance.

Distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react - for example using a mobile phone, adjusting the radio or talking to passengers. Like tiredness, drugs and alcohol, a distraction acts on the reaction time and so on the thinking distance, leaving the braking distance unchanged.

concepts.term: Measuring reaction time: the ruler drop method
concepts.def: One student holds a ruler vertically with the zero mark between the open thumb and finger of a second student, then releases it without warning. The catcher closes their fingers as soon as they see it move. The distance the ruler falls is measured and converted into a time using a conversion chart, because the ruler is in free fall. A shorter fall means a shorter reaction time.

concepts.term: Measuring reaction time: computer methods and typical results
concepts.def: Reaction time can also be measured with a computer or tablet program in which the user clicks or taps as soon as a shape appears or a sound is played; the machine times the response itself, so the experimenter's own reaction time cannot creep into the result. Typical classroom results are about 0.2 s to 0.3 s, at the fast end of the 0.2 s to 0.9 s range.

Repeat the test several times for each student, identify any clearly anomalous result and leave it out, then calculate a mean of the rest. Keep everything else the same - the same ruler, the same starting gap between the fingers, no countdown before the drop - so that any difference between students is due to reaction time and not to the way the test was run.

concepts.term: Judging the effect of a factor on thinking distance from data
concepts.def: To evaluate how a factor such as tiredness, alcohol or a phone call affects thinking distance, compare thinking distances measured at the same speed. Dividing a thinking distance by the speed converts it back to a reaction time, which allows results taken at different speeds to be compared fairly.

The braking distance of a vehicle can be affected by adverse road and weather conditions. Adverse road conditions include wet or icy conditions. They reduce the grip between the tyres and the road, so the vehicle travels further before it stops. They have no effect on the driver's reaction time, so the thinking distance is unchanged.

Braking distance is also increased by poor condition of the vehicle. Poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres - for example worn brake pads that cannot produce the full braking force, or tyres with too little tread to clear water from the road surface.

concepts.term: Estimating stopping distance at typical speeds
concepts.def: Estimate the thinking distance from thinking distance = speed x reaction time, using a reaction time of about 0.7 s for an alert driver. Estimate the braking distance from the braking deceleration using v2 - u2 = 2 a s, which is given in the exam; a typical family car on a dry road decelerates at about 6.5 m/s2. At 13 m/s (about 30 mph) that gives roughly 9 m + 13 m = 22 m, and at 27 m/s (about 60 mph) roughly 19 m + 56 m = 75 m.

Plotted against speed, thinking distance is a straight line through the origin, while braking distance is a curve that rises ever more steeply. The total stopping distance curve therefore also becomes steeper as speed increases. When two vehicles are plotted together, the one whose line lies higher needs the greater distance to stop at every speed.

concepts.term: Work done by the braking friction force
concepts.def: When a force is applied to the brakes of a vehicle, work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases. Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the vehicle to the thermal store of the brakes; none of it is destroyed.

The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance. The work done by the brakes is the braking force multiplied by the braking distance, and it must equal the kinetic energy of the vehicle; so if the distance is fixed, a vehicle with more kinetic energy needs a larger force.

concepts.term: Braking force, deceleration and its dangers
concepts.def: The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration of the vehicle. Large decelerations may lead to brakes overheating and/or loss of control. Overheated brakes become less effective, and a vehicle that skids can no longer be steered.

concepts.term: Estimating the force in a deceleration
concepts.def: (HT only) Estimate the deceleration first, either from acceleration = change in velocity / time taken, or from v2 - u2 = 2 a s, which is given in the exam. Then use resultant force = mass x acceleration, F = m a, which must be recalled. A typical family car has a mass of about 1000 kg to 1500 kg, so an emergency stop at about 6.5 m/s2 needs a braking force of roughly 7000 N to 10 000 N.

Because stopping distance rises with speed, and rises further in wet or icy conditions or with worn brakes or tyres, safe driving means leaving a gap big enough to cover the whole stopping distance and cutting speed when conditions are poor. Speed limits, minimum tyre tread depths and brake testing all exist because those factors change how far a vehicle needs in order to stop.

mcqs.q: A driver sees a hazard ahead and brings the car safely to rest. What is the stopping distance of the car?
options: The thinking distance added to the braking distance.
The distance travelled once the brakes are applied.
Twice the thinking distance, as the two parts match.
The distance travelled during the reaction time.
mcqs.explain: The specification defines stopping distance as the sum of the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time and the distance travelled under the braking force.

mcqs.q: A car is driven faster along the same road, and the braking force the brakes can produce is unchanged. What happens to the stopping distance?
options: Only the braking distance grows; thinking distance is fixed.
Only the thinking distance grows; braking distance is fixed.
It rises: both the thinking and braking distances grow.
It stays the same, because the braking force is unchanged.
mcqs.explain: Thinking distance = speed x reaction time, so it grows with speed, and a faster car has more kinetic energy for the same braking force to remove, so the braking distance grows too.

mcqs.q: A driver with a reaction time of 0.70 s is driving at 20 m/s when a hazard appears. What is the thinking distance?
mcqs.explain: Thinking distance = speed x reaction time = 20 m/s x 0.70 s = 14 m.

mcqs.q: A car's speed doubles from 15 m/s to 30 m/s. The driver's reaction time and the braking force are unchanged. What happens to the two parts of the stopping distance?
options: Thinking distance doubles; braking distance rises about four times.
Thinking distance doubles and the braking distance is unchanged.
Thinking distance is unchanged and the braking distance doubles.
Both the thinking distance and the braking distance simply double.
mcqs.explain: Thinking distance is proportional to speed. The brakes must do work equal to the kinetic energy, which is proportional to speed squared, so with the force fixed the braking distance quadruples.

mcqs.q: Stopping distance is plotted on the vertical axis against speed on the horizontal axis for one car. What shape is the graph?
options: A curve that gets steeper, as braking distance grows fastest.
A straight line from the origin, as distance follows speed.
A horizontal line, because the braking force does not change.
A curve that flattens off, as the brakes work harder at speed.
mcqs.explain: Thinking distance contributes a straight line, but braking distance grows with speed squared, so the total curves upwards and its gradient increases with speed.

mcqs.q: Stopping distance against speed is plotted for a car and for a loaded lorry on the same axes. The lorry's line lies above the car's line at every speed. What does this show?
options: At any given speed the lorry comes to rest more quickly.
The lorry's heavy load makes its driver's reaction time longer.
The lorry is always driven faster than the car on that road.
At any given speed the lorry needs a longer distance to stop.
mcqs.explain: The vertical axis is the distance needed in order to stop, so the higher line is the vehicle that needs more distance from the same speed.

mcqs.q: Which range gives the typical values of human reaction time?
options: 1.0 s to 3.0 s
0.5 s to 1.5 s
0.2 s to 0.9 s
mcqs.explain: These are the typical values given in the specification, and they match measured classroom results of about 0.2 s.

mcqs.q: Which of these would increase a driver's thinking distance at a given speed?
options: The road ahead is covered with ice and slush.
The tyres are worn below the legal tread depth.
The driver is tired at the end of a long shift.
The car is loaded with heavy luggage and cases.
mcqs.explain: Tiredness is one of the factors the specification names as affecting reaction time, and thinking distance = speed x reaction time.

mcqs.q: A ruler drop test is used to measure a student's reaction time. Which statement about the method is correct?
options: The number of centimetres the ruler falls is the reaction time.
The catcher is told exactly when the ruler will be released.
The distance the ruler falls is measured and converted to a time.
A stopwatch times the fall, avoiding any human reaction error.
mcqs.explain: The ruler falls freely under gravity, so the measured fall distance is converted into a reaction time using a chart or the free-fall relationship.

mcqs.q: A class measures reaction times using the ruler drop test. Which result is typical for a student?
options: About 2.00 s
About 0.20 s
About 1.20 s
About 0.02 s
mcqs.explain: A typical fall of around 20 cm corresponds to about 0.2 s, at the fast end of the 0.2 s to 0.9 s range.

mcqs.q: One student's five ruler drop results are 0.19 s, 0.21 s, 0.20 s, 0.55 s and 0.20 s. How should these results be treated?
options: Treat 0.55 s as anomalous; take the mean of the other four.
Take the smallest value, as that is the true reaction time.
Take the mean of all five, as no result can be left out.
Take the range of the values and quote that as the result.
mcqs.explain: 0.55 s lies far outside the tight spread of the other readings, so it is identified as anomalous and excluded, and the mean of the remaining four is quoted.

mcqs.q: Data for one driver at 13 m/s show a thinking distance of 9 m when alert and 15 m after drinking alcohol. What do these data show?
options: The alcohol has raised the driver's reaction time by about 6.0 s.
The alcohol has raised the reaction time by about 0.5 s.
The alcohol has raised the braking distance by about 6 m.
The alcohol has raised the driver's reaction time by about 1.7 s.
mcqs.explain: 9/13 = 0.69 s and 15/13 = 1.15 s, so the reaction time has risen by about 0.46 s, which rounds to 0.5 s.

mcqs.q: Which of these increases the braking distance of a car?
options: Rain has made the road surface wet and slippery.
The driver is tired at the end of a long trip.
The driver has taken a drug causing drowsiness.
A radio is playing loudly inside the moving car.
mcqs.explain: Wet conditions are named in the specification as adverse road conditions; less grip between tyres and road means the car travels further under the braking force.

mcqs.q: Poor condition of a vehicle can increase its braking distance. Which pair of parts does this cover?
options: The brakes and the engine.
The brakes and the tyres.
The brakes but not the tyres.
The engine and the gearbox.
mcqs.explain: The specification limits poor condition of the vehicle to the vehicle's brakes or tyres: worn pads reduce the braking force and worn tyres reduce grip.

mcqs.q: On an icy road, drivers are advised to leave a much bigger gap to the vehicle in front. Which statement best explains this advice?
options: The ice lengthens the driver's reaction time and thinking distance.
The ice stops the brakes from being able to grip the wheel.
The ice lengthens the braking distance, so more space is needed.
The ice makes the vehicle travel faster than the speedometer shows.
mcqs.explain: Ice is an adverse road condition that reduces grip between the tyres and the road, so the vehicle travels further under the braking force and the whole stopping distance grows.

mcqs.q: A car is travelling at 27 m/s. The driver's reaction time is 0.70 s and the car decelerates at 6.5 m/s2 while braking. Estimate the stopping distance.
mcqs.explain: Thinking distance = 27 x 0.70 = 19 m. Braking distance from v2 - u2 = 2 a s is 27 x 27 / (2 x 6.5) = 56 m. The total is about 75 m.

mcqs.q: A car is slowed by applying its brakes. Which description of the energy transfer is correct?
options: Friction in the brakes destroys the kinetic energy of the car.
The brakes store the kinetic energy and return it later on.
The kinetic energy is transferred to the road by the hot tyres.
Work done by friction cuts the kinetic energy and heats the brakes.
mcqs.explain: Work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases.

mcqs.q: A lorry brakes hard several times while descending a long hill. What happens to the temperature of its brakes?
options: It falls, because the lorry is losing its kinetic energy.
It rises, but only because the engine is working hard.
It stays constant while the lorry is still moving.
It rises, because work is done against friction at the brakes.
mcqs.explain: Each stop transfers kinetic energy into the thermal store of the brakes through the work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel.

mcqs.q: Two identical cars must each be brought to rest in a braking distance of 30 m. One is travelling at 15 m/s, the other at 30 m/s. What can be said about the braking forces needed?
options: Both need the same force; only the distance differs.
The faster car needs the greater braking force.
The faster car needs a smaller, longer-lasting force.
Both cars need exactly the same braking force.
mcqs.explain: Force x braking distance must equal the kinetic energy removed. Over the same 30 m, the car with more kinetic energy needs the larger force.

mcqs.q: A car of mass 1200 kg is travelling at 20 m/s and must stop in a braking distance of 40 m. The work done by the brakes equals the car's kinetic energy. What average braking force is needed?
mcqs.explain: Kinetic energy = 0.5 x 1200 x 20 x 20 = 240 000 J. Work done = force x distance, so force = 240 000 / 40 = 6000 N.

mcqs.q: A driver presses the brake pedal harder, which increases the braking force on the car. What happens to the car's motion?
options: Its deceleration falls, so it slows down more gently.
Its deceleration is unchanged; the brakes just act longer.
Its deceleration is unchanged; only the distance falls.
Its deceleration rises, so it slows down more sharply.
mcqs.explain: The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration of the vehicle, as resultant force = mass x acceleration.

mcqs.q: Which pair of effects are the dangers that a very large deceleration may lead to?
options: The brakes may cool too fast and then seize up.
The engine may overheat and the car may stall.
The brakes may overheat and control may be lost.
The brakes may wear out and need replacing.
mcqs.explain: These are exactly the two dangers the specification names: large decelerations may lead to brakes overheating and/or loss of control.

mcqs.q: A lorry driver brakes hard again and again while descending a long, steep hill. Why is this dangerous?
options: The brakes overheat and become less able to stop the lorry.
The engine overheats because it works against the brakes.
The brakes cool so quickly that they seize onto the wheel.
The tyres heat up, which makes them grip the road better.
mcqs.explain: Each stop transfers energy to the thermal store of the brakes. Repeated large decelerations overheat them, which is one of the dangers the specification names.

mcqs.q: (Higher Tier) A car of mass 1000 kg slows from 20 m/s to rest in a distance of 25 m. Use v2 - u2 = 2 a s to estimate the average braking force on the car.
mcqs.explain: 0 - 400 = 2 x a x 25 gives a = -8 m/s2, and resultant force = mass x acceleration = 1000 x 8 = 8000 N.

mcqs.q: (Higher Tier) A car of mass 1200 kg makes an emergency stop from 13 m/s, coming to rest in 4.0 s. Estimate the average braking force on the car.
mcqs.explain: Acceleration = change in velocity / time = 13 / 4.0 = 3.25 m/s2, so force = mass x acceleration = 1200 x 3.25 = 3900 N.
